name: Matthew
v: When Jesus finished saying all this, he turned to his disciples.
"Two days from now—Passover. And the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified."
At that very hour, the chief priests and the elders of the people were gathering in the courtyard of Caiaphas, the high priest,
plotting how to seize Jesus by stealth and kill him.
"Not during the festival," they said. "The crowd will riot."
Meanwhile, in Bethany, Jesus was at the home of Simon the leper,
when a woman approached him with an alabaster jar of perfume—extravagant, priceless—and poured it over his head as he reclined at the table.
The disciples saw it and were furious. "What a waste.
This could have been sold for a fortune and given to the poor."
Jesus knew exactly what they were thinking. "Why are you giving this woman a hard time? What she's done for me is beautiful.
The poor will always be with you. I won't.
When she poured this perfume on my body, she was preparing me for burial.
I'm telling you—wherever this gospel is proclaimed, in all the world, what she just did will be told. Her memorial."
Then one of the Twelve—Judas Iscariot—went to the chief priests.
"What will you give me if I hand him over to you?" They counted out thirty pieces of silver.
From that moment on, he was watching for his chance.
On the first day of Unleavened Bread, the disciples came to Jesus. "Where do you want us to prepare the Passover for you?"
"Go into the city, to a certain man," he said. "Tell him: 'The Teacher says, My time is close. I'm keeping the Passover at your house, with my disciples.'"
They did exactly what Jesus told them. They got the Passover ready.
Evening came. He took his place at the table with the Twelve.
As they were eating, he said it: "One of you is going to betray me."
They were devastated. One after another: "Surely not me, Lord?"
He answered, "The one who dipped his hand into the bowl with me—he's the one who will betray me.
The Son of Man goes the way it is written about him. But the man who hands him over—better for that man if he had never been born."
Judas, the betrayer, said, "Surely not me, Rabbi?" Jesus answered, "You said it."
While they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, gave it to the disciples. "Take. Eat. This is my body."
Then he took the cup, gave thanks, handed it to them. "All of you—drink.
This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many, for the forgiveness of sins.
I'm telling you—I won't drink from the fruit of the vine again until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom."
They sang a hymn and went out to the Mount of Olives.
Then Jesus told them: "Tonight—every one of you will fall away because of me. It's written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.
But after I am raised, I'll go ahead of you into Galilee."
Peter answered, "Everyone else may fall away because of you—I never will."
Jesus said, "I'm telling you the truth. Tonight, before the rooster crows, you'll deny me three times."
Peter insisted, "Even if I have to die with you, I will never deny you." All the disciples said the same.
Then Jesus went with them to a place called Gethsemane. "Sit here while I go over there and pray."
He took Peter and the two sons of Zebedee with him. Grief crashed into him. Anguish.
"My soul is drowning in sorrow—I'm dying with it. Stay here. Keep watch with me."
He went a little farther, fell on his face, and prayed: "My Father, if it's possible, take this cup away from me. Yet not what I want—what you want."
He came back to the disciples and found them sleeping. He said to Peter, "So—you couldn't keep watch with me for one hour?
Stay awake. Pray, so you don't fall into the test. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak."
He went away a second time and prayed: "My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it—your will be done."
He came back. Again, sleeping. Their eyes were too heavy.
He left them, went off again, prayed a third time, the same words.
Then he came to the disciples and said, "Still sleeping? Still resting? Look—the hour has arrived. The Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of sinners.
Get up. Let's go. Here comes the one who's betraying me."
He was still speaking when Judas arrived—one of the Twelve—and with him a mob, swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and elders of the people.
The betrayer had given them a sign: "The one I kiss—that's him. Arrest him."
He walked straight up to Jesus. "Hello, Rabbi." And he kissed him.
Jesus said, "Friend—do what you came to do." Then they closed in on Jesus, seized him, took him.
One of those with Jesus reached for his sword, drew it, struck the high priest's servant—cut off his ear.
Jesus said to him, "Put your sword back where it belongs. Everyone who picks up the sword dies by the sword.
Do you think I can't call on my Father, and he'd send me—right now—more than twelve legions of angels?
But then how would the Scriptures be fulfilled, saying it must happen this way?"
Then Jesus said to the crowd, "You've come out with swords and clubs to capture me, like I'm some kind of bandit? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you didn't lay a hand on me.
All of this is happening so that the writings of the prophets will be fulfilled." Then every disciple abandoned him and ran.
Those who had arrested Jesus took him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and elders had gathered.
Peter followed at a distance, all the way to the high priest's courtyard. He went inside and sat with the guards, waiting to see how it would end.
The chief priests and the whole council were trying to find false testimony against Jesus so they could put him to death.
They couldn't find any, though many false witnesses came forward. Finally two stepped up
and said, "This man said, 'I can tear down the temple of God and build it back in three days.'"
The high priest stood. "You have no answer? What about this testimony against you?"
Jesus said nothing. The high priest said, "I charge you under oath by the living God—tell us. Are you the Messiah, the Son of God?"
Jesus said, "You said it. But I tell you all—from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, coming on the clouds of heaven."
The high priest tore his robes. "Blasphemy! Why do we need any more witnesses? You heard the blasphemy yourselves.
What's your verdict?" They answered, "He deserves death."
Then they spat in his face. They punched him. Others slapped him
and said, "Prophesy for us, Messiah—who hit you?"
Meanwhile, Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. A servant girl came up to him. "You were with Jesus the Galilean too."
He denied it in front of all of them. "I don't know what you're talking about."
He went out to the gateway, and another girl saw him. She said to the people there, "This one was with Jesus of Nazareth."
Again he denied it, this time with an oath: "I do not know the man."
A little later the bystanders came over to Peter. "You're definitely one of them—your accent gives you away."
Then he started cursing and swearing: "I do not know the man." Immediately a rooster crowed.
And Peter remembered what Jesus had said: Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times. He went outside and wept—wept until he couldn't breathe.

com.d:
# Matthew 26: The Hour When Love Meets Its Deepest Cost

Matthew 26 records the sacred and terrible hours when Jesus moves toward the cross with full knowledge of what awaits—a passage that unveils both the costliness of redemption and the steadfastness of a love that cannot be shaken. Here we witness the conspiracy of enemies, the betrayal of a friend, and the anguish of a Savior who chooses obedience over escape.

The chapter begins with religious leaders plotting Jesus's death, yet immediately cuts to a woman anointing His feet with costly perfume—a moment of profound worship amidst hostility. Jesus defends her generous act, recognizing that she grasps what others miss: He is preparing for His burial. Even in celebration, He carries awareness of suffering ahead. This juxtaposition teaches us that devotion and sorrow, joy and sorrow, often walk together in the Christian life.

Judas's betrayal for thirty pieces of silver represents one of Scripture's darkest moments. Yet Jesus does not flee or rage; instead, He gathers His disciples for a final meal, where He institutes the communion that would forever bind His death to our redemption. When He identifies the betrayer, He does so with sorrow, not surprise—He knew who believed and who would not.

Gethsemane reveals Jesus's humanity in a way that comforts struggling disciples everywhere. "My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death," He confesses. The Son of God, fully human, wrestles with what lies ahead, yet submits: "Not as I will, but as you will." This is not blind obedience but chosen obedience, chosen in the darkness, chosen in genuine anguish.

The arrest, trial, and denial that follow show how quickly courage crumbles—Peter's denials echoing across the courtyard like a bell of human failure. Yet even Peter's breaking becomes part of a larger story of grace.

What would it mean for you to follow Jesus not just in moments of clarity, but through genuine darkness and uncertainty, trusting that His love holds even when everything feels lost?
com.s:
Matthew 26 constitutes a pivotal narrative unit within the First Gospel, marking the transition from Jesus's public ministry and eschatological discourse to the passion narrative proper. This chapter, likely composed in the 80s CE for a predominantly Jewish-Christian audience, demonstrates Matthew's characteristic concern for fulfillment of Scripture and his portrait of Jesus as the obedient Son who willingly embraces his divinely appointed destiny.

The chapter opens with Jesus's fourth and final passion prediction (vv. 1–2), employing the verb *paradidōmi* ("to hand over" or "to betray"), which functions as a Leitwort throughout the chapter, appearing in connection with Judas's treachery, the religious authorities' scheming, and ultimately God's sovereign purpose. This semantic richness captures the theological tension between human culpability and divine providence that pervades Matthean soteriology.

The anointing at Bethany (vv. 6–13) presents interpretive challenges regarding its relationship to parallel accounts in Mark 14 and John 12. Matthew follows Mark closely but emphasizes the woman's act as preparation for burial (*entaphiasmon*), foreshadowing the imminent death while simultaneously elevating her deed to paradigmatic status within gospel proclamation.

The institution of the Lord's Supper (vv. 26–29) contains Matthew's distinctive addition of "for the forgiveness of sins" (*eis aphesin hamartiōn*) to the cup saying, explicitly connecting Jesus's death to atonement theology and echoing the programmatic statement of 1:21. The term *diathēkē* ("covenant") evokes both Exodus 24:8 and Jeremiah 31:31–34, situating Jesus's sacrifice within Israel's covenantal framework while inaugurating its eschatological renewal.

Gethsemane's portrayal (vv. 36–46) reveals Matthew's high Christology paradoxically expressed through Jesus's genuine anguish. The prayer addresses God as *Pater* ("Father"), reflecting intimate relationship, while Jesus's submission—"not as I will, but as you will"—exemplifies the righteousness Matthew consistently demands. Peter's threefold denial (vv. 69–75) forms a tragic counterpoint to his earlier protestations, with his bitter weeping (*eklausen pikrōs*) suggesting the possibility of restoration that chapter 28 will confirm. Matthew thus weaves together themes of betrayal, covenant, and costly discipleship that define Christian existence.
com.p:
Matthew 26 unfolds during the final week before the crucifixion, approximately AD 30-33, as Jesus approaches the culmination of His earthly ministry in Jerusalem. This chapter stands at the hinge point of all human history—the moment toward which every sacrifice, every prophecy, and every divine promise had been pointing since the Fall in Eden. We are witnessing the transition from anticipation to fulfillment, from shadow to substance, as the Lamb of God prepares to accomplish what no animal sacrifice could ever achieve.

The chapter opens with Jesus declaring that the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified at Passover—a statement of staggering typological significance. Fourteen centuries earlier, God commanded Israel to slay a lamb without blemish, apply its blood to their doorposts, and watch as the destroyer passed over their homes. That original Passover was never meant to be the final word; it was a prophetic portrait awaiting its true subject. Now the true Passover Lamb announces His own slaughter, transforming an annual memorial into eternal redemption.

The woman who anoints Jesus with costly perfume at Bethany performs an unwitting prophetic act, preparing His body for burial before the rulers have even finalized their conspiracy. Her extravagant worship stands in stark contrast to Judas's calculated betrayal for thirty pieces of silver—the exact price Zechariah prophesied for the rejected Shepherd of Israel. The prophet's ancient words find their terrible fulfillment in the darkened heart of one who shared bread with the Master.

At the Last Supper, Jesus reinterprets the Passover meal itself, lifting the bread and cup to declare them His body and blood of the new covenant. Jeremiah had promised a new covenant written on hearts rather than stone; now its ratification draws near through the shedding of innocent blood. Every communion thereafter becomes a proclamation of His death until He returns.

In Gethsemane, the second Adam succeeds where the first Adam failed. Where Adam reached for forbidden fruit in a garden of delight, Jesus surrenders His will in a garden of agony, sweating drops like blood as He embraces the cup of divine wrath. His arrest, the scattering of disciples, Peter's denial, and the mockery of His trial all fulfill Scripture with precision—the Shepherd struck, the sheep scattered, the Righteous One numbered with transgressors.

For the church living between advents, this chapter summons us to the Table of remembrance, to costly worship, and to watchful prayer, knowing that the same Lord who drank the cup of judgment will soon return to drink it new in His Father's kingdom.
